title: Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership
description: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNvidia
body: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg speaks during the Meta Connect event in Menlo Park, California, Sept. 23, 2026.Minh Connors | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesNvidia has said it will invest $3 billion in Meta after the social media and AI giant announced plans to raise $95 billion to support its investments in artificial intelligence infrastructure.Meta on Monday said it would initially raise $35 billion in underwritten public equity offerings, before raising an additional $60 billion with an at-the-market program.The announcement said Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, and Broadcom were interested in purchasing up to $5 billion in shares.Nvidia deepens Meta tiesNvidia announced its investment on Tuesday, adding that Meta would expand Vera Rubin and Vera CPU deployment, and that the two companies would deepen their partnership on Muse, the social media giant's AI agent that launched last month."AI agents represent a new computing paradigm — software that understands our goals, reasons, uses tools and gets work done on our behalf," said Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang in a statement.Jensen Huang, CEO of NVIDIA, presents new NVIDIA Vera Rubin DSX Pod Full-Stack Modular AI Factory as he gives a keynote address at the Berlin GPU Technology Conference (GTC) on October 21, 2026 in Berlin, Germany.Sean Gallup | Getty Images"This changes how we use computers, from operating applications to working with intelligent agents.""We're excited to keep working with NVIDIA to deliver the best personal agents and frontier models for billions of people," said Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg.Both companies' shares were flat in premarket trading on Tuesday.Nvidia has been rapidly building up stakes in companies powering the AI boom, investing in OpenAI, Anthropic, Intel and XAI. The chip giant has participated in 121 investment rounds so far this year, according to Dealroom, up from just 13 in 2022.

schema.headline: Nvidia to invest $3 billion in Meta as tech giants deepen AI partnership

title: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote
description: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn ext
body: An El Al Boeing 737-958(ER) takes off from Barcelona-El Prat Airport in Barcelona, Spain, on Aug. 27, 2025. Joan Valls | Nurphoto | Getty ImagesAn extremely tight race into Israel's election Tuesday, has some citizens flying back into the country to cast their votes.Israel doesn't allow votes from abroad, except from those serving in the country's diplomatic missions. As many as 80,000 Israelis living outside the country are expected to come back to vote in Tuesday's election, according to estimates from one group helping to organize citizens living outside the country. Israel has about 7.3 million eligible voters, according to the Washington-based International Foundation for Electoral Systems."While not a large block, the 80,000 that may return home to participate could make a big difference in the final count of a very tight election," said Yael Shomer, a professor of political science at Tel Aviv University.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu speaks during a press conference, amid the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, in Jerusalem, March 19, 2026. Ronen Zvulun | ReutersIn Israel's first election since 2022, Benjamin Netanyahu of the Likud party, who has served as Prime Minister for 18 years over three separate periods, is facing top challenger Gadi Eisenkot, the former chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, who heads the Yashar party. Both would likely need backing from potential coalition partners in order to win. Polls are extremely tight heading into Tuesday's election. Issues like security, already a major decider for Israelis, have gotten even more contentious with the Iran war in full swing. The exemption of some ultra-Orthodox men from conscription is also causing a great divide in Israeli society, while Prime Minister Netanyahu is still working on a controversial plan that would give the governing coalition more control over the judiciary.25 October 2026, Israel, Tel Aviv: Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot addresses attendees from behind a lectern emblazoned with party slogans during an election rally. Erik Marmor | Picture Alliance | Getty Images"All elections in Israel are energetic, but because this one will have such a meaningful impact on the future of the country it has been especially hard fought," Shomer said. "This election is really about how we see our future, voter turnout will be very high."Voter turnout in 2022 was just above 70% according to Israel's Central Elections Committee. Pollsters believe it could reach as high as 87% this time. Among foreign service workers serving in embassies and consulates outside of Israel, voter turnout was 90%. According to The Central Elections Committee, that number is usually closer to 70%.In order to help those living abroad come back to cast votes, an organization called Fly & Vote was set up by the America-Israel Democracy Coalition, a U.S.-based group which was originally created in 2023 to stop the effort by Likud to reform the judicial system. While organizations and political parties are prohibited from paying for any kind of transportation for people inside or outside of Israel, Aid Coalition has found other ways to facilitate the voting. Fly & Vote, which has been funded by private donations, chartered a flight for Israelis living in Portugal and bought blocks of tickets for flights from the New York area. Anyone on the flights had to pay for their own seats. "Israelis who don't live here still have a stake in what we do, and we want to help them," said Ora Peled-Nakash, the group's co-founder. "We don't take a political position though and we don't tell anyone how to vote, we just help them cast their ballot." Travelers will also have plenty of commercial options.For decades El Al was the only Israeli airline to fly routes from the U.S. to Israel. Arkia started offering flights last year and Israir earlier this year. Legacy U.S. carriers United and Delta are also flying to Israel again after suspending flights due to the war with Iran. Germany's Lufthansa flies to Israel from Europe and British Airways is scheduled to re-start flights this week. What's more, the price is in line with what it would be during normal times, Peled-Nakash said. There were still a few seats left on El Al flights from JFK or Newark airports ranging from $1,300 to $2,500 as of Sunday, according to research from CNBC.After years of political instability that saw five elections between 2019 and 2022, Tueday's election result could help shape Israel's political, security and economic direction for years to come. But it also shows how politically divided the country has become.

schema.headline: Israeli election draws tens of thousands of citizens flying back to vote

title: HSBC shares slump on revenue miss, lender announces share buyback of up to $1 billion
description: Dado Ruvic | ReutersEurope's largest bank HSBC on Tuesday announced a share buyback of up to $1 billion and reported third-quarter pretax profit that
body: Dado Ruvic | ReutersEurope's largest bank HSBC on Tuesday announced a share buyback of up to $1 billion and reported third-quarter pretax profit that largely met analysts' estimates.Revenue at HSBC rose to $18.6 billion from $17.8 billion in the same period last year, while banking net interest income rose 6%, alongside the bank clocking higher fee income form its corporate and institutional banking and wealth business. HSBC's London-listed shares dropped 6.5% in early European deals Monday, putting them on course for the worst session since Apr. 3 2025. Earlier, shares in Hong Kong dropped 2.95% following the earnings release, which saw the bank approve a third interim dividend of 10 cents per share.Citi analysts cited a "mixed set of results," noting a 2% miss on revenue expectations but an 18.8% return on tangible equity in the year to date — significantly ahead of its medium-term guidance of around 17%.Here are HSBC's third-quarter results compared with the consensus estimates compiled by the bank.Pre-tax profit: $9.63 billion vs. $9.69 billion expected Revenue: $18.6 billion vs. $18.93 billion expectedThe bank's third-quarter profit before tax increased 32% from a year earlier to $9.6 billion, also reflecting the absence of $1.4 billion in legal provisions recorded in the same period last year. Higher revenue and lower credit losses also supported earnings. The bank's net interest income rose to $9.3 billion in the third quarter, supported by deposit growth and reinvestment of its "structural hedge at higher yields."Meanwhile, operating expenses decreased 12% year on year to $8.8 billion, largely due to non-recurrence of legal provisions recorded a year earlier. Excluding notable items, expenses rose amid inflation and higher spending on technology. Looking ahead, HSBC maintained its forecast for banking net interest income of at least $46 billion in 2026, while reiterating its target for return on average tangible equity — a metric for assessing profitability — of 17% or higher for 2026 through 2028, excluding notable items.The bank also expects revenue to grow annually through 2028, targeting 5% growth that year compared with 2027, excluding notable items and on a constant currency basis.HSBC said it remains on track to deliver operating expense growth of approximately 1% in 2026 on a target basis, although strong business performance could lead to additional performance-related pay and modestly higher cost growth.The bank said it had bought back $1 billion in shares announced at its interim results, and expects to complete another $1 billion in buybacks before its full-year 2026 results.HSBC is reportedly considering significant job cuts in its U.K. wealth management business, as part of a broader push to adopt artificial intelligence.

schema.headline: HSBC shares slump on revenue miss, lender announces share buyback of up to $1 billion

title: NBA enters prediction markets with Kalshi, Polymarket partnerships
description: Tari Eason #17, Amen Thompson #1 of the Houston Rockets and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers go up for the rebound during the game during R
body: Tari Eason #17, Amen Thompson #1 of the Houston Rockets and Austin Reaves #15 of the Los Angeles Lakers go up for the rebound during the game during Round One Game Five of the 2026 NBA Playoffs on April 29, 2026 at Crypto.Com Arena in Los Angeles, California. Adam Pantozzi | National Basketball Association | Getty ImagesThe NBA is embracing prediction markets for the first time by naming leading platforms Kalshi and Polymarket as its preferred exchanges. Through the agreements, the league said there will be "significant integrity" protections for NBA markets, including limitations on which types of event contracts can be featured and information-sharing requirements regarding suspicious trades. "Protecting the integrity of the game is our top priority," said Scott Kaufman-Ross, NBA head of media distribution and partnerships in a press release. "These partnerships represent an important step in establishing a framework that creates new opportunities to engage our fans."As part of the announcements, the league also signed a memorandum of understanding with the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, the federal agency that asserts prediction markets are under its purview. The agreement seeks to maintain the integrity of both the NBA and event contract markets, the memo said, through exchanges of information. The NBA is the latest league to create partnerships with the booming prediction markets industry, which has seen much of its growth over the past year come from the popularity of its sports-related offerings. The NHL in October 2025 announced partnerships with both Kalshi and Polymarket, while the MLB announced a relationship with the latter company in March. Those same contracts, though, are under fire by states across the country, who argue that the offerings amount to sports betting and should be regulated by them. Platforms and the CFTC argue that event contracts are swaps, a type of derivative, and thus are regulated at the federal level. Courts across the country have delivered conflicting rulings on the issue, and many expect the Supreme Court will likely be needed to resolve the dispute. "The NBA is one of the most influential sports leagues in the world, and we're excited to work together to bring fans closer to the game," said Ari Borod, president of sports business development at Polymarket, in the press release.  As preferred exchanges, Kalshi and Polymarket get rights to use NBA intellectual property along with marketing and licensing rights. watch now"It's an exciting time for both NBA fans and Kalshi users," Adam Barrick, head of sports partnerships at Kalshi, said in the release. "The relationship we've built together reflects a shared mindset that prioritizes fan engagement, innovation and safety."The NBA's move on Monday now leaves the NFL as the outlier among major American sports leagues when it comes to prediction markets. Earlier this month, the NFL in an amicus brief to the Supreme Court said that sports-related event contracts should be regulated by the states rather than the CFTC. The league added that it's not opposed to the markets, but rather thinks they should have more guardrails.At the time, Kalshi told CNBC it had tried to work more closely with the NFL, but that the league hadn't engaged. Adam Silver, the commissioner of the NBA, though, took a different approach on the regulation question in an interview with CNBC's Contessa Brewer in early October. "From at least the NBA standpoint, we have roughly 40 different jurisdictions regulating us right now," he said. "So to have a consistent policy nationally, I think would be in our best interest."— CNBC's Jessica Golden contributed reportingDisclosure: CNBC and Kalshi have a commercial relationship that includes customer acquisition and a minority investment.

title: Investors are doing just as well this year by shunning AI. How to invest if the tech trade keeps fizzling
description: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on October 19, 2026. Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty I
body: Traders work on the floor of the New York Stock Exchange (NYSE) at the opening bell in New York City on October 19, 2026. Angela Weiss | Afp | Getty ImagesA version of the S&P 500 without AI briefly pulled ahead of the traditional index this year and is now neck-and-neck as investors rotate into other areas of the market.A proprietary Goldman Sachs index tracking the S&P 500 without stocks classified as "AI enablers" was up 12.4% through Oct. 22, edging ahead of the standard S&P 500's 12% gain. The Goldman index is now neck-and-neck with the S&P 500 as tech rallied in Monday trading. Tech and AI-related companies make up about 45% of the S&P 500. That heavy weighting has helped power the index for years, but it's turned into a liability lately; the S&P 500 tech sector is down about 7% this month while other sectors have held up. Investors have soured on debt and equity issued by companies like CoreWeave and Oracle. Shares of Meta Platforms sank almost 7% Thursday after it outlined more plans to spend heavily on capex and issue additional shares.Companies supplying power and equipment for the buildout have been hit hard — names like GE Vernova,  Bloom Energy, Vistra and Quanta Services all suffered steep declines during the recent selloff. Goldman, which launched the measure earlier this year with S&P, uses the S&P 500 as its starting universe and excludes companies perceived to be enablers of AI before applying S&P 500 Index weighting methodology to the remaining universe of companies. AI trade loses steamThe ex-AI index lagged the S&P 500 for most of the year as investors continued to favor chipmakers, cloud-computing companies and other firms benefiting from heavy AI spending. However, that advantage has been narrowing and it disappeared last week. Meanwhile, investors are rotating into defensive areas. ETFs like State Street Consumer Staples Select Sector SPDR ETF, State Street Health Select SPDR ETF and State Street Utilities Select Sector SPDR ETF  are up 7% to 10% this month. Energy is ahead 10% too, though that's more related to the war in Iran.  Some analysts recommend sticking with non-AI companies for diversification and protection against more pain in tech. The "AI pendulum has swung back in favor of non-AI exposure over the last two weeks," Oppenheimer technical analyst Ari Wald said in a note on Oct. 24. Two industries that Oppenheimer favors now are commercial services and insurance. The firm upgraded those industries to overweight last week, recommending Republic Services, Cintas, Verisk Analytics, Broadridge Financial Solutions, MetLife and Arthur J. Gallagher.Berkshire Hathaway is also capitalizing on the rotation out of tech. Its Class B shares are up 8% this month, though it's still lagging behind the S&P 500 this year. Berkshire owns a wide swath of operating companies, including insurance giant Geico and Burlington Northern Santa Fe railroad. It also has a $364 billion stock portfolio including companies like Apple, Coca-Cola, Alphabet and Bank of America. That diversification may help Berkshire continue to outperform if the tech sector drags down the S&P 500. Trivector Research sees potential in "non-tech compounders." Healthcare giant Eli Lilly is one idea. The stock is up 22% on the strength of Lilly's weight-loss drugs. The company has more in the pipeline, including a next-generation obesity drug that Lilly plans to file for FDA approval early in 2027.  Viking Holdings, a cruise operator, is also proving durable. The company said on its August earnings call that 40% of its river capacity and 60% of its ocean capacity was already booked for 2027. "Based on recent events, we've seen our guests have proved to be resilient and are continuing to book 2027 and future seasons," the company told investors. Viking stock is up 15% this year but it may still have upside. The average Wall Street target is $109, above recent prices around $82. Barclays recently upgraded the cruise operator to overweight with a $102 target, citing the company's "compelling risk/reward."

title: The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House
description: watch nowPresident Donald Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024, stitching together his base with unusual support from some tr
body: watch nowPresident Donald Trump forged an extraordinary coalition to win office in 2024, stitching together his base with unusual support from some traditional Democratic groups like Hispanics and young people. It was enough to sweep the battleground states and catapult him into office for a second term.The latest CNBC All-America Economic Survey shows that coalition is now seriously weakened.Since the beginning of his second term, the president's net approval rating among Latino voters has dropped from -22 to -38, and declined from -28 to -53 among 18- to 34-year olds. Black respondents have moved from -55 to -67.Among all registered voters, his approval has fallen from -7 at the start of his term to -19 in the most recent survey. The decline in the president's approval carries over into the Republican base. Approval from self-described Trump voters has fallen from a net +85 in 2025 to a net of +65. Net approval has even turned negative in the South, from +2 in 2025 to -20 in the latest survey. The results of the latest poll show why Republicans are facing an uphill battle in the midterm elections next week. Trump is not on the ballot — but his presence will be felt. Read the full survey results here.To be sure, Republicans in the survey still give the president an 82% approval rating, and those who say they identify with the MAGA movement are at 90%. But interest in the election is 10 points lower among Republicans than it is for Democrats, and in tight races, the party that better turns out its voters will have an advantage.The survey of 1,000 registered voters nationwide found 44% of respondents say their biggest worry if Republicans control Congress is allowing President Trump to operate beyond his constitutional power. By contrast, 28% say their biggest worry for Democratic control is passing policies of Democratic Socialists. For either party's control, registered voters worry that Congress won't do enough to bring down prices.The survey was conducted Oct. 14-18, and was co-led by Democratic pollster Hart Research Associates and Republican pollster Public Opinion Strategies. It carries a margin of error of plus or minus 3.1 percentage points. As a second-term president who had skipped four years between terms, Trump's arc of approval has followed an unusual path. The president left office above water on the economy, with 48% approving and 41% disapproving — high numbers for a president whose last year was overwhelmed by the Covid pandemic.But there was no second-term honeymoon. Trump was immediately underwater in his economic approval rating in the April 2025 CNBC survey. That could have reflected immediate public discontent with the tariff regime and resulting market turmoil. The president's economic approval rating remained negative through most of his first year.The bottom dropped out, however, with the launch of the Iran war. By April 2026, the president's net economic approval rating was plying depths last seen under President Joe Biden amid the aftermath of the pandemic, when the country was facing high inflation and elevated unemployment.In the first quarter of this year, Trump's net economic approval dropped 10 points to -21. It has plunged to -31 in the latest survey. Economic disapproval rose to 65%, the highest for any president CNBC has measured back to President Barack Obama, and one point higher than Biden's worst showing. The survey shows increasing disapproval of Trump's handling of inflation. Over the same time, shooting of Americans by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers began to dominate headlines, eroding support for one of the president's major policy initiatives.The survey this quarter appeared to pick up growing frustration with a host of issues, from immigration to the economy, among those demographic groups that had supported the president in unusual numbers in 2024, with sharp declines in economic and overall approval among Latinos, young people and those in the $50,000 to $75,000 income group.Most ominously for the president, views on the economic outlook fell 22 points for Republicans. Though still net positive, it was the lowest level of economic optimism for Republicans since Biden.These downbeat views on the economy do not automatically translate to votes for Democrats. The survey showed a 7-point preference for Democratic control of Congress, a 3-point gain from the July survey. While Republican economic pessimism grew, so did their preference for a Republican-controlled Congress, from 85% in July to 87% in October.Blue-collar workers show how the president has maintained his base amid growing concern about the economy. Their net economic approval of the president has plunged 22 points to -15 from the beginning of Trump's term to now. But their overall presidential approval remains +6, just a four-point drop. They still prefer a Republican-controlled Congress by 21 points, though that is down from 33 points in July.The days and weeks leading up to the election have seen the president barnstorming through red states, a sign of concern with the base's enthusiasm. But it also creates the possibility that he could fire up his base and bring them out to stanch potential Democratic gains. The survey shows that the extra votes from the coalition that put Trump in the White House in 2024 would be a reach for Republican congressional candidates in 2026.

schema.headline: The arc of Trump: How the president lost the coalition that put him in the White House

title: Jim Cramer warns this overlooked danger could threaten the market rally
description: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Mon, Oct 26 20266:09 PM EDTKey PointsCNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that a flood of massive IPOs and ca
body: Monday - Friday, 6:00 - 7:00 PM ETMad MoneyPublished Mon, Oct 26 20266:09 PM EDTKey PointsCNBC’s Jim Cramer warned that a flood of massive IPOs and capital raises could drain money from the stock market, threatening its rally.Anthropic’s highly anticipated IPO filing on Monday came after companies have already raised $148 billion through public offerings this year, raising concerns that investor demand may struggle to keep pace with new stock issuance.watch nowCNBC's Jim Cramer warned Monday that a wave of massive initial public offerings and capital raises could threaten the bull market.Anthropic, the company behind Claude, filed its IPO prospectus Monday, moving one of Wall Street's most anticipated public debuts a step closer. Investors have long awaited public offerings from AI leaders Anthropic and OpenAI, but Cramer said that their potentially massive fundraising needs could strain an already crowded market. With $148 billion raised through IPOs so far this year, he fears the influx of new shares could outstrip investor demand and derail the rally."Politics can weaken the bull, higher rates can choke it, but if you want to slay the darn thing, use the IPO lance and stab it again and again," the "Mad Money" host said. "It just gets weaker and weaker until it is weak enough to be slaughtered with the ease of a bad quarter, a rate hike and a run on the margin bank." Cramer emphasized that his concerns aren't about the viability of AI itself. Unlike the speculative internet startups that collapsed during the dot-com bust in 2000, many of today's leading technology companies have established businesses and genuine demand for their products. "This time around the companies are real. They tend to make big money. We trusted them before this moment. We will trust them after," he said. But Cramer sees one troubling similarity between the two periods: the enormous amount of capital being raised. During the dot-com boom, a flood of stock offerings eventually exhausted investors' buying power, contributing to the market's collapse. Supply outpaced investor demand. He fears a similar dynamic could emerge as companies including Meta, Alphabet, SpaceX and Oracle tap capital markets. Cramer warned that these massive fundraising efforts could absorb investor dollars that might otherwise flow into the S&P 500 and other stocks, putting pressure on the broader market even as corporate fundamentals remain strong. Cramer's Charitable Trust, the portfolio run by CNBC's Investing Club, owns shares of Meta and Alphabet."I think both the debt and the equity markets are running out of money," he said. That means the market could run out of the money companies need to finance their ambitions before investors see the payoff. "I am not calling a top," he said. "I am just saying that I do not like what I see."watch now

title: Anthropic's IPO puts power in the hands of founders, giving everyday shareholders little voice
description: Prospective Anthropic investors better buckle up, because the AI company's seven co-founders are firmly in the driver's seat. The Amodei siblings — An
body: Prospective Anthropic investors better buckle up, because the AI company's seven co-founders are firmly in the driver's seat. The Amodei siblings — Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and President Daniela Amodei — and five others will be the "sole members" of "Founder LLC," a new entity that will hold 50.1% of the voting power of the company's outstanding shares. The structure gives them "the ability to determine the outcome of all matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally for the foreseeable future," Anthropic said in its IPO prospectus on Monday.  The arrangement will also limit the power and influence of institutional and retail investors, who will have to put their trust in a small band of artificial intelligence engineers and researchers as the company marches toward a trillion-dollar-plus market cap. Anthropic has long tried to establish itself as the more safety-conscious AI lab, and it's created a structure designed to give its founders the ability to preserve that long-term mission, even as it enters the world of quarterly financial reports."Our governance structure is likely to have the effect of limiting the likelihood of an unsolicited merger proposal, unsolicited tender offer, or proxy contest for the removal of directors," Anthropic said in the filing. "As a result, our governance structure may make it more difficult to replace our directors and management and may have the effect of depriving our stockholders of an opportunity to sell their shares at a premium over prevailing market prices."Anthropic's "novel capital and corporate governance structure" serves as another layer of complexity for investors to consider as they pore over the company's prospectus, which includes more than 90 pages of risk factors. Anthropic highlighted a number of political challenges, data center moratoriums and the company's effort to balance safety and commercial objectives as potential risks. For some investors, founder control is a defining characteristic of generational tech companies. Byron Deeter, a partner at Bessemer Venture Partners, told CNBC Monday that "when you have great leadership," investors are often comfortable giving early management and founders governance into the public market. Bessemer backed Anthropic at a $14 billion valuation, and Deeter said it's the biggest investment on a cost basis in the firm's 116-year history.SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has retained roughly 85% of the voting power at his rocket maker, while Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg has around 60% of the voting power at the social media giant. Both executives have positioned themselves as indispensable to their companies, which can also put them at odds with their investors. "There are some unusual elements to these things when they occur, but for category-defining, industry-defining opportunities, you want teams to be able to think long term," Deeter told CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Monday. "And there are a lot of benefits to being able to do that so teams can focus on true innovation, and not be month-to-month, or even quarter-to-quarter."Sam Altman remains a powerful figure at competitor OpenAI, especially since many of his original co-founders have departed. Unlike Amodei, Altman has no direct equity in his company and OpenAI's current structure doesn't offer a similar voting bloc like the one Anthropic created through Founder LLC. Aside from the Amodeis, Anthropic's founding team includes Tom Brown, chief compute officer; Jack Clark, head of the Anthropic Institute; Jared Kaplan, chief science officer, Sam McCandlish, chief architect; and Christopher Olah, head of interpretability research efforts.Anthropic's Founder LLC builds on its existing status as a public benefit corporation, which means it's required to balance the financial interest of stockholders, the best interests of those affected by its conduct and its "Company Purpose," which is to facilitate the "responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."In addition, Anthropic introduced an independent governance body called the "Long-Term Benefit Trust" in 2023, which has the authority to elect and remove the majority of the company's board of directors. The LTBT will exercise that authority using a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, which "does not otherwise have voting rights on matters submitted to stockholders generally," according to the prospectus. The LTBT currently includes Christopher Stubbs, an experimental physicist, Ben Bernanke, the former chair of the Federal Reserve, Neil Buddy Shah, CEO of the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and Richard Fontaine, a national security expert. All the trustees are "financially disinterested" from Anthropic, according to the filing. Anthropic is considered a "controlled company," according to Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements, because the LTBT has the authority to elect the majority of its board. Anthropic said it plans to list on the Nasdaq under ticker symbol "ANT."Anthropic's co-founders will have the authority to elect the company's remaining board members through their capacity within Founder LLC. It said Monday that it believes its co-founders are "distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission." The company said the voting power of Founder LLC and its LTBT are "not derived from or proportionate to economic interests" in the company, and won't be diluted or otherwise reduced. The company said its capital structure will concentrate voting power within these two entities for "the foreseeable future." "Moreover, the LTBT, Founder LLC, and our individual co-founders may have interests that differ from yours and may vote in a way with which you disagree and that may be adverse to your interests," Anthropic said. title: Federal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates steady in October. Here's what that means for consumers
description: watch nowThe Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its upcoming October meeting — even as higher energy costs complicate th
body: watch nowThe Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its upcoming October meeting — even as higher energy costs complicate the inflation outlook and put additional pressure on household budgets.The consumer price index, a broad measure of inflation, rose again in September, bringing the annual inflation rate up to 3.7%. Surging oil prices stemming from the U.S. war with Iran also helped drive September's producer price index higher. On Friday, Brent crude oil was trading at a five-month high before falling slightly. The Fed raised rates by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75% to 4% last month, its first hike since 2023. But fed funds futures last priced in less than a 10% chance the central bank will raise rates by another quarter point at its meeting this week, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool. Nearly 75% expect at least one hike by year-end."Inflation is still the No. 1 problem in the U.S. economy, and there are a lot of signs it is getting more broad-based," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "For consumers, it means really high borrowing costs for the foreseeable future."However, "given that it's right before an election," she added, "they won't hike in October."Read more CNBC personal finance coverageTrump's executive order aims to lower mortgage costs. What it means for buyersIf Elon Musk gifts SpaceX stock through Trump Accounts, it will come with a catchRoth conversions aren't for everyone. When the 'juice' isn't worth it: Top advisorThe affordability crisis isn't hitting all voters equally. Here's whyCNBC's Financial Advisor 100: Best financial advisors, top firms for 2026 rankedCNBC Elite Advisors: Top ultra-high net worth wealth management firms for 2026The central bank's upcoming meeting comes just days before the midterm elections and marks the final word on the pace of inflation in the U.S. before voters head to the polls, which could impact how much power each political party has in Washington.In previous election cycles, the Fed has mostly maintained its charted course, research shows. The four times the Fed raised rates near a midterm — 1978, 1982, 2018 and 2022 — were all tied to rising inflation, according to Mark Shore, director and economist at CME Group.  Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh has expressed a commitment to bringing inflation down to the Fed's 2% target. "If the Fed holds, markets could question the Fed's inflation-fighting credibility," said Bank of America economist Aditya Bhave in a research note on Oct. 23. How the Fed affects your moneyThe Fed's benchmark interest rate determines what banks charge one another for overnight loans. That rate then influences a wide range of consumer borrowing and savings rates. However, while higher interest rates can help ease inflationary pressures, they also raise borrowing costs in the near term, adding to the affordability crunch many households already face.Shorter-term rates are closely tied to the prime rate, which is typically 3 percentage points above the federal funds rate. Longer-term borrowing costs, meanwhile, are driven more by inflation expectations and broader economic conditions."Higher longer-term rates are doing more damage to consumer wallets, as they've risen more than short-term rates, and are weighing heavily on refinancing activity, homebuying and vehicle sales," said Mark Zandi, chief economist at Moody's. "Higher short-term rates also hurt, but mostly by raising rates on credit cards, consumer finance loans and home equity lines."Most credit cards carry variable rates that move closely with the Fed's benchmark rate. As a result, if the Fed leaves rates unchanged, credit card APRs are likely to remain near current levels. The average interest rate on a new credit card offer is now 23.96%, according to LendingTree.Mortgage rates, by contrast, are influenced more by Treasury yields and the economic outlook. The yield on the 10-year U.S. Treasury, which serves as a benchmark for many long-term loans, has been near 5%, helping keep the average rate on a 30-year fixed mortgage close to 7.4%, according to Mortgage News Daily.Auto loan rates are shaped by several factors, including the Fed's benchmark rate. With financing costs still elevated, many car buyers are taking on larger loans and extending repayment terms to cope with affordability challenges, according to Edmunds.Federal student loan rates are fixed for the life of the loan, but rates for new borrowers are already higher in the current academic year based on the results of the 10-year Treasury note auction held in May.Savings rates tend to track changes in the federal funds rate, which is a rare upside to the higher-for-longer rate outlook. Because the Fed has kept rates elevated, savers continue to benefit from relatively attractive yields on high-yield savings accounts and other deposit products.Subscribe to CNBC on YouTube.

schema.headline: Federal Reserve is likely to hold interest rates steady in October. Here's what that means for consumers

title: Elon Musk says more than 200 neoclouds face 'guppy-level death'
description: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outsid
body: SpaceX CEO Elon Musk attends a press briefing held by President Donald Trump with AI executives following a meeting on artificial intelligence, outside the West Wing of the White House in Washington, Sept. 29, 2026.Finn Gomez | Getty ImagesElon Musk said that more than 200 neocloud companies could collapse, sending shares in those companies whipsawing.Nebius, Iren and CoreWeave all fell in early trading, adding pressure to a sector already facing investor concerns about debt-fueled expansion and whether the large AI infrastructure buildout will generate returns. The stocks all rebounded later in the day."As of the past few weeks, debt markets have almost entirely shut off access to money for any company that doesn't have substantial revenue independent of AI data centers," Musk, CEO of SpaceX and Tesla, said on a post on X on Sunday."That means the 200+ neoclouds are going to see guppy-level death and consolidation. Some will make it through, but not many," he added.Musk's SpaceX operates its own data centers through which it sells computing capacity. SpaceX is a direct competitor to the neoclouds which also rent compute. Stock Chart IconStock chart iconCoreWeave, Nebius and Iren shares over the past five days.Musk was replying to a post on X by Chamath Palihapitiya, the founder of Social Capital, who laid out his views on the state of the data center buildout. He suggested that there will be "a lot of partially stranded compute and compute sitting in inventory in 2027 than is currently forecasted," which will be "bought and paid for but effectively underearning (below total cost of capital) or collecting dust.""2027 will be a turbulent year because it will clear out a bunch of wrong/bad bets. It will also be a consolidation year for a few," Palihapitiya said.Neocloud stocks have taken a hammering over the past month, with CoreWeave and Nebius down more than 30% while Iren has tanked 40%. The sell-off started earlier this month after the spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps hit levels generally viewed as signs of distress. The yields on CoreWeave's bonds also climbed. Investors have grown jittery over companies that are borrowing heavily to fund the purchase of expensive Nvidia chips, build data centers, and rent out computing power. watch nowNvidia, neoclouds defend demandNvidia, an investor in several neoclouds, looked to shore up the sector last week at its GTC event in Berlin, Germany. In an interview with CNBC, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the demand for neoclouds is "off the charts.""What is missing in the middle is the working capital to fuel that growth… because there's just so much demand across so many sectors of AI, there's a scarcity of capital," Huang said."The demand of the capital is much greater than the availability of the capital. That's going to get solved," he added.Marc Boroditsky, chief revenue officer at Nebius, distanced his company from concerns surrounding CoreWeave, saying "we're not carrying the kind of debt that they are," in an interview with CNBC. Boroditsky said that if the AI infrastructure company brought its 2027 capacity online, it would sell out. And there could be "the same type of dynamic" in 2028.watch nowIren Co-CEO Daniel Roberts also defended demand."We understand the increased focus from investors, but when we're talking from customers, nothing has changed. The demand is still there," Roberts told CNBC last week. "Next year, we are having conversations with customers covering multiples of all the capacity we possibly bring online, and in the last month or so, 2028 is now coming into focus. But the demand is there," he added.

schema.headline: Elon Musk says more than 200 neoclouds face 'guppy-level death'

title: The 'stablecoin sandwich': Why speeding up payments isn't so simple, according to Mastercard
description: CHONGQING, CHINA - JULY 29: In this photo illustration, a person holds a smartphone displaying the logo of Mastercard Inc. (NYSE: MA), a global paymen
body: CHONGQING, CHINA - JULY 29: In this photo illustration, a person holds a smartphone displaying the logo of Mastercard Inc. (NYSE: MA), a global payments and technology company, with the company's distinctive red and yellow overlapping circles visible in the background, on July 29, 2025 in Chongqing, China. (Photo illustration by Cheng Xin/Getty Images)Cheng Xin | Getty Images News | Getty ImagesStablecoins could offer faster and more efficient payments, but realizing their full potential requires further development of the infrastructure supporting them, according to Mastercard.Stablecoins, a type of cryptocurrency designed to keep a steady value via a peg to an asset like the U.S. dollar, could be attractive for certain remittance corridors and less commonly traded currency pairs, Matthew Driver, executive vice president of services for Asia Pacific at Mastercard, told CNBC in an interview."You don't want to have a 'stablecoin sandwich,'" Driver said, referring to a slow on-ramp into stablecoins, a fast transaction in the middle and a slow off-ramp back into fiat currency. That won't necessarily translate into faster payments, he said.Connecting real-time payment systems to stablecoin exchanges on both ends of a transaction could help speed up payments, but "you still need to enable the infrastructure," he said, adding that market participants need to be able to use the technology effectively.Opportunities for stablecoin adoption could vary across markets. In Singapore, where retail payments are already highly efficient, stablecoins may have fewer applications in consumer transactions, while corporate payments could offer greater opportunities, Driver said.He also pointed to smart contracts as a potential use case for corporate payments, allowing transactions to be executed when certain conditions are met.Interest in stablecoins has increased following the establishment of the U.S. GENIUS Act, Driver said.His comments come as Mastercard expands its involvement in digital assets, including through its acquisition of stablecoin infrastructure provider BVNK, which was completed in August. Earlier this month, Mastercard and BVNK launched Global Money Platform, designed to help banks, fintechs and businesses manage payments involving traditional currencies and stablecoins through a single application programming interface.Beyond payment speed, Mastercard is also looking to incorporate blockchain and identity data to establish the same level of trust expected across other payment systems, Driver said.

schema.headline: The 'stablecoin sandwich': Why speeding up payments isn't so simple, according to Mastercard

title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers
description: A Dollar General store in New York, US, on Tuesday, June 3, 2025. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Trade Commission said Monday that it
body: A Dollar General store in New York, US, on Tuesday, June 3, 2025. Adam Gray | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Federal Trade Commission said Monday that it filed a lawsuit along with 20 states accusing Dollar General of charging customers more than the prices it displays on shelves, price tags and in advertisements. Shares of Dollar General dropped about 4% after the FTC announced the lawsuit.The complaint alleges that thousands of Dollar General stores have "taken advantage of vulnerable shoppers by extracting millions of dollars in unlawful overcharges with insufficient safeguards to prevent the practice." It also argues that Dollar General has received "tens of thousands" of complaints from consumers about charging higher than advertised prices, but that it has not implemented policies to address the problem. The states joining the FTC in the lawsuit are Alabama, Arizona, Arkansas, California, Connecticut, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Mississippi, Nebraska, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin."Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last," said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC's Bureau of Consumer Protection. Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment.The suit comes as shoppers look for discounts while they face elevated food and gas prices. Officials across the political spectrum also aim to show their efforts to protect consumers from high costs ahead of the midterm election next week.

schema.headline: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, alleging retailer overcharged shoppers

title: Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates this week — but stay hawkish: CNBC survey
description: Kazuo Ueda, governor of the Bank of Japan (BOJ), speaks during a conference hosted by the bank's Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies in Tokyo,
body: Kazuo Ueda, governor of the Bank of Japan (BOJ), speaks during a conference hosted by the bank's Institute for Monetary and Economic Studies in Tokyo, Japan, on Tuesday, May 27, 2025. Kiyoshi Ota | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe Bank of Japan is expected to keep the policy rate unchanged at 1.25% at the end of its two-day meeting on Friday, according to a CNBC survey, with the possibility of a hike very much alive in the coming months.All 16 respondents expect the BOJ to stand pat, given the bank raised rates last month to their highest level in 31 years. All respondents said they expect the BOJ to set the stage for a rate hike in December or January next year, as domestic inflation and wages continue to rise. Macroeconomic factors support the BOJ's additional policy tightening, said Homin Lee, senior macro strategist at Lombard Odier. "But there may not be sufficient consensus in the policy board for successive rate hikes given the fragility in the domestic bond market," he added. Sosuke Nakamura, an economist at Citi Research, said he sees no clear signs of inflation accelerating to a degree that would justify consecutive rate hikes. Japan's core inflation, excluding fresh foods, for September rose 2.1% from a year earlier, reaching its highest this year as a weak yen raises import costs and elevated energy costs feed through to higher prices, even as government subsidies absorb rising costs of energy for consumers. Japan's inflation-adjusted wages rose for the eighth month in a row in August, climbing 1.5% from a year earlier, according to the most recent government data, signaling potential wage-growth-driven inflation as well.Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama reportedly told lawmakers last week that Japan was "on the cusp of shifting to a period of sustained inflation driven by rising wages," while acknowledging that higher import costs were also pushing up prices.The BOJ is expected to declare that its "underlying inflation" target of 2% has been met at this meeting, according to reports by Reuters and The Japan Times. Yen and yields Ryutaro Kimura, senior fixed income strategist at BNP Paribas Asset Management, said he was waiting to see if the BOJ changes its phrasing about inflation in the monetary policy statement this week from "underlying CPI inflation has been approaching 2 percent" to it "has reached 2 percent."As for the yen, nine respondents expect it to trade between 157 and 158 against the greenback over the next one month. Respondents' outlook for the three-month yen target was more scattered, ranging from 150 to 160."BOJ normalization, higher domestic yields and shifting institutional flows should gradually narrow the rate differential and pull capital back toward Japan," said Masahiko Loo, senior fixed income strategist at State Street Investment Management. But he added, "Elevated U.S. yields should prevent a straight-line yen rally."The yen strengthened against the dollar, and Japanese government bond yields fell last week due to safe-haven demand amid a sell-off in AI stocks —  a reversal from earlier in the month, when Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi's spending plans and a global bond sell-off pressured those assets. Nine respondents said they expect the yield on the benchmark 10-year JGBs to be between 3% and 3.1% by the end of the year, up from the current 2.809%. Seven respondents said they expect the yield on the 30-year JGB to rise to 4% to 4.1% from 3.829% as of Tuesday. That forecast comes as analysts expect the BOJ will resume tightening after an anticipated pause in October. Takuji Aida, chief Japan economist at Credit Agricole, said the next rate hike is likely to happen in January, when the BOJ is scheduled to release its quarterly outlook report that assesses economic activity and prices. Thirteen respondents said they expect a terminal rate, or the level at which the BOJ is expected to stop its tightening cycle, of 1.75% to 2% by around mid-2027. Macroeconomic data shows the policy rate is closer to the neutral level of 2%, the BOJ's inflation target, said Masato Koike, senior economist at SOMPO Institute Plus. But "given the state of the Japanese economy and the need to avoid excessive downward pressure on growth, I expect the BOJ to stop raising rates at around 1.75%," Koike said. The CNBC survey was conducted from Oct. 14  to 26 among 16 economists and analysts.— CNBC's Lim Hui Jie and Sri Jegarajah contributed to this report.

schema.headline: Bank of Japan is expected to hold rates this week — but stay hawkish: CNBC survey

title: From Wall Street to Silicon Valley, Anthropic IPO poised to have massive 'trickle-down effect'
description: Dario Amodei, Anthropic's co-founder and CEO, appears on a panel at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on Jan. 23, 2025.Stefan Wermuth |
body: Dario Amodei, Anthropic's co-founder and CEO, appears on a panel at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, on Jan. 23, 2025.Stefan Wermuth | Bloomberg | Getty ImagesThe tech industry needs this to go well. So does Wall Street.Anthropic's IPO filing on Monday puts the Claude creator in position to pursue what could be the largest initial stock offering in history. Investors are already measuring the 5-year-old company's potential market cap in the trillions, putting it in a category with the world's most valuable companies. It's a critical moment for the whole tech sector, as the artificial intelligence boom has been largely driven by two companies: Anthropic and OpenAI. The latter has confidentially filed to go public, but has said a debut likely won't take place until 2027.Meanwhile, the stock market is showing signs of jitters on the AI trade. Neoclouds and data center companies have been getting pummeled, prompting Australia's Firmus to withdraw its IPO plans and for SK Hynix's U.S.-based Solidigm unit to do the same. Now, all eyes turn to Anthropic, which is betting that investors will look past over $80 billion in losses in the first half of the year, and see the 14-fold increase in revenue as a reflection of seemingly insatiable demand for the company's leading models and services."If it underperforms expectations, it'll be a little bit of a house of cards," said Jai Das, co-founder of Sapphire Ventures whose career in tech investing dates to the 1990s.watch nowAnthropic's business is deeply entwined with tech megacaps. Close to half its revenue comes from Claude being sold through cloud divisions at Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet, which all hold investments in the company. In the IPO, some $77 billion in notes can be issued to Amazon, Broadcom and Google, while Microsoft and Nvidia agreed to invest $15 billion as the company builds up its computing capacity. Chips from Nvidia, Advanced Micro Devices, Amazon and Google are powering Anthropic's development. Cloud providers are ratcheting up capital expenditures to meet demand, and memory manufacturers are fighting shortages to prioritize AI chips. And there's the debt factor. Alphabet, with its investment-grade credit rating, committed to backstopping Anthropic for a data center in Texas. Broadcom, which helps Google develop chips for AI labs, is creating financing pools to help Anthropic and OpenAI deploy high-performance models, CEO Hock Tan told analysts earlier this year.For public market investors, more than one-third of the value of the S&P 500 comes from tech's trillion-dollar companies, which are all, to varying degrees, going deep in AI. Beyond that, there are software giants like Adobe and Salesforce that have integrated with Anthropic's Claude assistant.Market reset?And in the private markets, check sizes have ballooned but IPOs are few and far between. Bessemer Venture Partners and Menlo Ventures both told CNBC that Anthropic is their biggest investment ever."If they don't perform well, they will become the bellwether for AI," said Brad Bernstein, a managing partner at growth equity firm FTV Capital. "Their valuation will reflect that performance variation, and then it'll just be a trickle-down effect to all the stuff going on with the excess capital that's getting poured into the venture AI world. Everything is going to have to sort of be reset."Anthropic will be the third company to go public with a valuation above $1 trillion, after Saudi Aramco and Elon Musk's SpaceX, which debuted in June. OpenAI could be the fourth. Revenue at Anthropic has been multiplying at a staggering pace as businesses adopt the company's coding and productivity tools. Second-quarter revenue soared to $11.56 billion from $787 million a year earlier. The company held almost $132 billion in cash, equivalents and short-term investments at the end of June. And after five quarters of operating losses, Anthropic reported $974 million in operating income for the second quarter. "It is, I think, better than feared," said Rohit Kulkarni, partner and chief AI officer at Burnham Park Capital Markets, referring to the financials. "There could have been more negative tidbits."JINAN, CHINA - JULY 17: In this photo illustration, the logo of Kimi K3 is displayed on a smartphone screen on July 17, 2026 in Jinan, Shandong Province of China. (Photo by VCG/VCG via Getty Images)Vcg | Visual China Group | Getty ImagesOne source of concern in some corners of the investing universe is the emergence of so-called open-weight models, which are cheaper for businesses to access and allow for customization and flexibility in terms of where users access the models.In the prospectus, the only two competitors Anthropic named were OpenAI and Google, though the company said it faces competition from a "broader set of model providers," including open-weight or open-source models.Anthropic says it's all very early, with Fortune 500 companies committing less than 0.1% of their total expenses to its models and services in the latest quarter. Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager at Founder ETFs, says that's part of the investment thesis."I think there's going to be room for frontier models like Anthropic and OpenAI and SpaceX, and I think there will be room for open-weight models," Monaghan said. "It's way too soon to say that one is going to disintermediate the other." With hyperscaler spending on AI infrastructure set to reach into the trillions of dollars, Sapphire's Das said there's understandable concern about a market glut. But he compares it to the telecommunications and dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when companies flooded the market with fiber-optic equipment. Eventually, the infrastructure got used, although plenty of companies went belly up in the interim.  "Long term, I don't think there is a lack of demand," Das said.  Downside risksA lackluster debut could push out OpenAI's offering even further and cause investors to rethink its lofty valuation. At the same time, rising interest rates mean it's getting costlier for companies to raise debt.David Trainer, CEO of financial research firm New Constructs, wrote in a report last month that the AI boom has been built on the view that cheap credit and access to the capital markets will be "readily available.""If AI liquidity dries up, and there are clear signs it is, we see large, 20%, downside risk in the S&P 500, with most of that concentrated in the valuation of AI-related stocks," Trainer wrote. Industry experts take a different approach, focusing on the power and rapid proliferation of the technology. Claude Opus 5.5 Max performs better than any other model on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, an industry benchmark.Snowflake CEO Sridhar Ramaswamy said the technology is only becoming more essential. "Anthropic and OpenAI have by now demonstrated their ability to stay at the frontier of AI and keep pushing innovation," Ramaswamy said. "They're incredible companies that are doing a big service to humanity by expanding the frontier of what is possible, and we are very much rooting for them to be public and very successful companies."Still, Snowflake is experimenting with low-cost open-weight models from China's Moonshot AI, DeepSeek and Zhipu."We spend a lot on internal AI because we want to get as much efficiency as we can," Ramaswamy said.WATCH: Seems like Anthropic will beat OpenAI to IPO, says FirstMark's Rick Heitzmannwatch now

schema.headline: From Wall Street to Silicon Valley, Anthropic IPO poised to have massive 'trickle-down effect'

title: Oil prices seesaw amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end Mideast conflict
description: A drone view shows fuel vessels docked at the Baniyas oil terminal in Baniyas, Syria, Oct. 12, 2026. Karam Almasri | ReutersOil prices inched higher T
body: A drone view shows fuel vessels docked at the Baniyas oil terminal in Baniyas, Syria, Oct. 12, 2026. Karam Almasri | ReutersOil prices inched higher Tuesday, reversing earlier losses driven by renewed diplomatic efforts to end the U.S.-Iran war and hopes of a de-escalation in the wider regional conflict that has seen Tehran-backed Houthis target Saudi Arabia. Futures for international benchmark Brent crude for December delivery rose 0.52% to $116.45 a barrel as of 4:57 a.m. ET. U.S. West Texas Intermediate futures for June rose 0.62% to $102.39 per barrel.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon Brent It follows talks between Saudi Arabia, Turkey, Pakistan and Iranian officials in Tehran on Monday, as they stepped up efforts to defuse tensions across the Middle East.Riyadh said the discussions were aimed at keeping diplomatic channels open and preventing another escalation in hostilities. The four countries agreed to continue to engage to advance regional peace and security, according to Iranian state media.The diplomatic push comes as U.S. President Donald Trump said in an interview with Fox News on Sunday that he was approaching a decision on whether to strike a deal with Iran or intensify military operations, suggesting that additional attacks remained an option.Representatives from Qatar, which has helped mediate negotiations between Washington and Tehran, also traveled to the Iranian capital on Sunday, Reuters reported.Stock Chart IconStock chart icon wtiProspects of a diplomatic breakthrough have helped temper fears of further disruptions to global energy supplies, putting downward pressure on crude prices.But earlier oil price losses were limited as the prospect of a lasting resolution appeared fragile, with Iran-backed Houthi militants continuing their attacks on Saudi Arabia over the weekend.—CNBC's Justina Lee contributed to the report.

schema.headline: Oil prices seesaw amid renewed diplomatic efforts to end Mideast conflict
